Uniform Title: Kulasāra Manuscript: NGMCP 4-137/vi Reel Number: A 40/11

Description: The manuscript is incomplete. It begins abruptly in the middle of the fourth chapter (*paṭala*) and continues from the eighth to the seventeenth chapter, where it ends abruptly. The *Kulasāra* is cited by non-dualist Kashmiri Śaiva authors and thus predates the eleventh century. It belongs to a genre of Kaula Tantras focused on the attainment of the direct experience of essential metaphysical principles and yogic powers through the practice of yoga and insight. Through knowledge of these principles, the Kaula yogi attains liberation while living (*jñānāvabhāsena jīvanmuktye vyavasthitaḥ*, fol. 33b) as well as numerous yogic powers. The text also focuses on the worship of Bhairava, the Goddess (*Devī*), and the host of Yoginīs. The initial chapters concern the four principles commonly mentioned in Kaula works: *piṇḍa*, *pada*, *rūpa*, and *rūpātīta*. Unfortunately, the manuscript is incomplete at this point. Chapter nine deals with the attainment of the pervasion of transcendent Śiva through the renunciation of *śakti* (9). The following chapter teaches the attainment of the supreme reality—the Ineffable, devoid of phenomenal qualities, immobile, and all-pervasive like the sky—through absorption into the space contained within the jar of the psycho-physical body (10). The next chapter treats transcendent *akula* and immanent *kula*, along with *kaula*, which is their union (11). Chapter twelve describes the ascent through the centers (*cakras*) of the body from the feet to the head. Corresponding to the spheres of the gross elements, these are the abodes of various types of Yoginīs described in the text and the harm they can inflict. The yogi must recognize them and be protected from them through devotion to the deity, fire, and the guru, as well as the practice of yoga; those who are immoral are consumed by them. The chapter concludes with a series of visualizations (*dhyāna*) intended to protect the yogi’s body (12). The subsequent chapter continues with similar concerns for protection and the overcoming of disease and death through the use of the Bhairava mantra and visualization of his form—which appears to be that of Svacchandabhairava—along with his attendant forms and consorts (13). The next chapter discusses non-duality in the sense of the absence of pure and impure regarding food and drink, as well as the defects of those who do not follow this path. It proceeds to discuss freedom from dualistic conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and the resulting purification of the mind and the sacrificial substances. This is applied first to the sacrificial meat and then to wine (14). Chapter fifteen deals with the conduct (*caryā*) of the Kaula adept (*vīra*). He should travel to the internal Kaula sacred sites (*pīṭha*, *kṣetra*) within the body following the vital breath rather than the external ones. There, he sports with the Yoginīs and worships them, doing so externally as well with a pure mind. The manner in which the pilgrimage is to be performed externally is described next. The final chapter deals with the Three Jewels of Śiva, Śakti, and the Self, their attainment, and the experience thereof.

There is no other modification there, for it is merely the manifestation of a fabrication; just as the space enclosed within a jar is moved here and there when the jar is moved.
Just as a jar does not carry space, so too the soul, which is like the sky, does not carry the body;
for the body is held here like a plantain stalk, resting upon the leaf of reality.
Therefore, when one abandons even that [notion of] "thatness," then the space-like state arises for one whose mind has entered into meditative cultivation— the formless self-knowledge.
Even for liberation, he has no longing; thus he attains liberation. That which is called liberation is indeed bodiless and formless.
Liberation is inconceivable and devoid of qualities; liberation is not accompanied by dissolution.
There is no place for liberation, nor can there ever be a path to it.
The view known everywhere as "equal liberation" belongs to those who profess liberation,
yet by whom external detachment has been practiced extensively while the self has not been extinguished.
Not even one among them exists here who has attained the state of form;
likewise, others too—whosoever they may be—who are free from passion, are likewise [situated].
And so they remain, just as Nirvana was first;
for the self, once extinguished, has gone to the state of hell.
It has not gone to that place on earth, nor does it remain right there.
Nor has anyone ever drunk poison without a basis;
likewise, one should grasp the detachment that has been taught as beneficial by the Guru.
For that reason, although there is a single, eternal, and beginningless entity,
it is considered external by those who propound liberation, wherein all things have come to an end.
Even detachment from this world brings happiness to sentient beings;
however, since that [detachment] does not exist there, one will have to perform penance for the body.
But when it is free from attachment, it is indeed non-conceptual; yet when possessed of attachment, it is bound. Just as the various forms of rivers cease once they have reached the ocean.
There they do not recognize one another's distinctions,
nor do others perceive any distinction therein in that water.
In that regard, while the rivers have reached their end, the great ocean remains as one;
likewise, the body is like a river, and nirvāṇa is like the ocean.
While you remain free from anger, the oceans and rivers indeed stand still;
for they attain a state of motionlessness and contentment when you are satisfied.
One does not perceive pleasure or pain, but grasps the qualities of auspiciousness;
for that which is a meditation upon non-existence becomes existence once it has been rendered supportless.
Having established the mind within the Self, one should not think of anything at all;
whether in the state of non-existence or existence, being free from fear, one remains absorbed in the state of Being.
The all-pervading one is to be understood as equal; there is no need for deliberation here.
How can there be the manifestation of non-existence? For that which is partless, how could there be a mind?
41a) If there is abiding in the state of non-conceptualization (amane), that is his state of nirvāṇa;
in that [state], all objective existents (bhāva) dissolve as if they were hidden while he is awake.
His consciousness is sufficient; by him the three-footed [path] has been leaped over.
Indeed, the filler is to be known as the imperishable; O Goddess, the well-considered is the syllable-less.
Through *kuṃbhaka*, he should know Śiva, who is beyond the perishable and the imperishable; having abandoned everything, established in *samādhi*, He is the object of the internal organ.
He who always finds that which is worshipped by yogis there— namely,
the tradition as it truly exists, correctly pointed out by the instruction of the Guru.
That very [reality], both internal and external, is the beginningless and imperishable Śiva.
The Goddess said:
O Hara, O Supreme Lord, having grasped existence within non-existence, I must understand the distinction between the imperishable and the perishable in this way.
By means of that consciousness alone, those free from conceptual construction are liberated;
they enter into that Śiva-principle which is identical with the Wielder of the Trident.
Śrī Bhairava.
O lady of excellent hips, through the partless [reality], one attains success without even effort;
having known the divided state as threefold, one shall not undergo birth again.
For the sake of attaining perfection through the method of emanation, and for liberation itself during reabsorption—
having understood both origination and dissolution, one undoubtedly attains perfection.
The Goddess said:
The origin and dissolution of beings, as well as their coming and going—I desire to understand this; O Blessed One, you should explain it to me.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess, O lady of lovely countenance, I shall now proclaim this great and excellent discourse concerning both origination and dissolution, for the sake of your pleasure.
Arising, effort, and dissolution are known as emptiness;
through both, the perfection of yoga is attained—no one who is bound is ever bound.
But he who is born from this very [source] shall not exist above nor below;
they say that he is spread out, residing within all living beings.
O Great Goddess, during the great night of merit and demerit, the movement of the prāṇa and apāna is dear to me; O Great Goddess, one should utter this "haṃsa," the two-syllabled mantra.
He who discerns this while the moon is in Mercury, having reached the further shore of reality,
is liberated from both birth and death; indeed, he is released from this entire world.
Who perceives the body as dead and the birth from one's own body? Without consciousness, there is nothing to be abandoned; how then could liberation occur for him?
One should always eat, O Goddess, when the impurity of death or birth has ceased;
one should always sacrifice, O Goddess, when the impurity of death or birth has ceased.
O Goddess, when birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka) have ceased, one should perform the favor [of worship].
Birth-impurity resides within the body, while death-impurity is likewise on the outside.
Furthermore, one should investigate individually that which resides within the body:
the origin and dissolution of the elements, as well as their coming and going.
For the sake of knowledge, one who knows reality becomes a master of reality when it arises;
the lower power is to be understood, while the two deities are established in *pratiṣṭhita*.
O Goddess, because she stands between those two, she is known as Mathanī;
she exists as the heat of the *haṃsa* during creation and dissolution, and as the state of dissolution itself.
Having thus understood the perishable and the imperishable, one enters the supreme reality;
the other, the supreme imperishable, exists as a single intrinsic nature.
One who knows the three principles becomes liberated and attains a state of mental equipoise;
having thus entered the reality, one shall never fall away from it again.
Having become Śiva himself and having directly realized the supreme object of knowledge, he cuts the tree from its root; once burnt, it acts like a withered stump.
Just as for one who has broken the lineage [of practice], action is the cause even in direct perception;
likewise, in every moment and in every action, the three times (past, present, and future) are fully operative.
The contemplation of all things from Śiva down to the earth constitutes omniscience;
the movement and vision of that supreme one abide as the perfection desired by others.
O Goddess, even in tens of millions of eons, its exhaustion does not occur;
this essence has been declared by me out of affection for you, and not merely as a matter of deliberation.
Upon realizing that reality, the cessation of all becoming arises;
for the Buddhas, there is the discernment of dissolution and disappearance, and the total destruction of delusion.
Having thus abandoned the abode known as the supremely pure, with the body free from all attachment, one awakens to the reality of purity.
Entering that primordial state which expands reality through contemplation,
one whose purpose is established through the course of the Kula practices meditates upon the state of being; there,
the body is dissolved by the rising radiance, and for one who has known all principles, the one all-pervading reality remains as its own inherent nature.
O Goddess, one who is rich in the threefold qualities of the family is truly liberated;
indeed, there is no other knowledge superior to mine here in this world.
[This applies] to the young one, in the great ocean of existence which is difficult to cross and terrible in form.
Having mounted the Kaula path, which is known to be enriched by the arts of the lineage, there is no wonder here in this awakening through the mouth of the Guru who bestows supreme love.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Kulasāra.
The illustrious Bhairavī said:
O Maheśvara, you have spoken of Akula, Kula, and Kaula;
by your grace, O Lord of the Gods, tell me so that I may understand them.
Bhairava said:
43b) O Goddess, Akula is the first; everything is situated as a surrounding enclosure.
It exists externally and internally, established within all beings as their own self.
I bow to that which is all-pervading, the creator of all, the omnipresent Maheśvara,
free from anything to be rejected or accepted, consisting of the ultimate reality, and immutable.
That is declared to be *akula* for which no *kula* exists;
*kula* is said to mean an aggregate (*saṃghāta*), O Maheśvarī, and that which has none is *akula*.
This one has no second; for he is indeed solitary and alone.
That state of being without a second is the supreme, which is comparable to the object of knowledge.
Thus, that which is the desire [of the Supreme] is called Sakula.
That supreme, all-pervading reality is established within it;
creation, maintenance, dissolution, and concealment are proclaimed to be therein.
Knowledge and action reside therein; therefore, that supreme Kula should be known.
By the mere will of the one desiring to conquer, this world of moving and unmoving beings has arisen.
Having performed all foundations without exception, she remains as the pervasive agent;
then, merged again into the supreme reality, they are established in that state of being armored.
44a) I shall now declare that state of being armored; listen, O large-eyed one!
It pervades everything without exception, from Śiva down to the very end.
She should be known as all-pervading and Maheśvarī because of her sovereignty;
she is formless, devoid of color, and indeed beyond misfortune, being of the nature of immortality.
It is accessible through the realization of one's own self, for otherwise it is difficult to attain;
it resembles the fiber of a lotus stalk, and likewise resembles the hair-tuft between the eyebrows.
But in every state, O Maheśvarī, because of its subtlety, it is merged into the Sūtra;
O beautiful one, it is merged into the principle of the *ūrṇā* at the end of all paths.
O Gaurī, because all limiting adjuncts have dissolved, she is like a crystal stone;
yet, like a well-washed white garment, she reveals all states of being.
O Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign is pure consciousness established in self-awareness;
that pure consciousness arises within pure consciousness and there again undergoes dissolution.
The minister is unawakened yet pervades all branches of learning;
she is the support for the supreme reality, like clarified butter produced from milk.
That which is called knowledge has the nature of pervasion; it bestows the realization known as knowledge.
O Goddess of Gods, established in reality, it is that very reality, yet it has entered into manifold states of being.
Whatever exists in the world, all that is born from the Kula;
she is declared to be the seventeenth digit (kalā), and of this there is no doubt.
Nourished by her, Soma, the bringer of nourishment to the world, became both manifest and unmanifest;
then, O illustrious one, he merged into Śivā.
O Dear One, the state of *kalā* has arisen in two ways, consisting of the Moon and the Sun;
it is endowed with sixteen *kalās*, along with the four *kalās* of the *golaka*.
It is joined with two cavities, hanging downward, and endowed with the twelve digits; the sun is situated above it.
But the grasper, O sinless one, remains among them and devours them simultaneously;
likewise, the grasping occurs with a distinction at every moment, as does the equinox.

O Great Goddess, they arise endowed with that which is to be known by means of a hundred thousand [verses]. O fair-browed one, this is Kulakaula; it is proclaimed as the process of manifestation (*kalana*).
O Goddess, by calculating the division of day and night for all embodied beings,
a man who knows Kula and Kaula shall attain Akula.
One who is established in this, intent upon the expansion of reality, is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
O illustrious lady, these four have been declared to be like jewels.
Neither for the sake of liberation nor for the sake of spiritual attainment, but like Ajagrīva eating slowly;
therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in Kulakaula.
The supreme reality is never obtained otherwise than through the cause of attaining the *akula*; for the attainment of the *kula* requires great effort.
This is difficult for all yogis to attain, yet it is easily obtained by those who have not disciplined themselves; without [proper] lineage, neither knowledge nor yoga itself can be realized.
O Maheśvarī, you do not possess accomplishment or the means of accomplishment, nor the extraction of mantras, nor even the defining characteristics of one's own nature; you do not perceive them.
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in the Kaula path alone,
which bestows a multitude of accomplishments for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Knowledge that produces immediate conviction and bestows great wonder—
having thus attained such knowledge, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Those who, though awakened by the descent of power (śaktipāta), reject the flood of nectar issuing from the mouth of the Guru— which bestows auspiciousness— after having tasted it, [are lost].
Those who disparage this supreme knowledge, which is difficult even for the gods to attain,
go to a terrible hell for as long as the dissolution of the earth lasts.
For one who has been initiated, [practices] from other tantras do not succeed;
instead, they are born into low births, possessed by the delusion resulting from that downfall.
Again and again they are seen in the hells, for which there is no atonement;
their fruit lasts for as many ages and intermediate kalpas as there are in that number.
If one consumes the *caru* of the Kaulas without restraint,
the spirits will harm him and his loss of fortune will occur.
Out of faith and with a pure mind, for the sake of seeking knowledge,
he will spread out feigned devotion and move about for the sake of his guru.
O Beloved, those born of noble lineage take away from him what has reached another's ear;
O Goddess of Gods, those lowest of men do not cause it to fall even by way of that region.
By that which is terrible, more terrible than the terrible, there is no doubt that it devours;
it is considered that Yoga destroys the unfolding of the effects of past karma (prārabdha).
When one falls into doubt even regarding a matter spoken by the Guru,
or concerning knowledge, one should perform worship and may even undergo the punishment of lying on a bed of thorns.
Just as a clay pot filled with water perishes when deprived of heat,
so too the yoga of *prārabdha* perishes due to its slackening.
Free from conceptual construction and doubt, devoted solely to the guru,
steadfastly established in knowledge alone, wise, firm-minded, and devoid of indolence.
46b) He attains accomplishment and liberation; here, the disciple attains accomplishment by this path.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Kulasāra.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of the gods, O Support of all, O Master of the world,
by your grace I have heard the stainless knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the pure state.
"That which is difficult for all yogis to attain has been realized by me;
today, O Lord of the Gods of gods, O Maheśvara, satisfaction has arisen within me."
"I remain here, O Lord of the gods, because you have shown me compassion;
now I wish to hear about the movement that consists of the deities."
O Lord of the Gods, how do those [energies] abide within the body?
And how should the yogis protect their own bodies from them?
Tell me all this in brief, O destroyer of desire.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess, this Kaulika knowledge is extremely secret;
it must be guarded with great effort, yet out of love for you, I shall speak it.
Listen attentively, O blessed lady, to this great and hair-raising account:
all the perfected ones (siddhas) and those possessing knowledge (vidyās), having been praised, each performed their respective rites within their own circles.
They sport with the divine worlds even of Hari and Brahmendra;
their command is all-ordaining, and they remain praised within my city.
O blameless one, I shall now briefly describe the fifth [house], the Libra, which is the goal; I shall explain their movements as they are situated within one's own body.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, having entered the earthly principle (pārthiva-tattva) located in the anus, the genitals, the tips of the nails, and the feet,
they arise as those who move upon the earth.
The door is this bloodless marrow; there is no doubt that it is semen and flesh.
Those situated therein cause it to move; remaining there, they become ninefold.
Having reached the cavity of the navel up to the throat,
they undoubtedly draw forth the cow-like [vital essence] that has arisen within the field of experience (gocaryā).
O Goddess of the Suras, having reached the third aperture of the face, those who abide in the body through that sequence arise from their own place.

O fortunate one, having reached the head, those born from the host of sky-faring goddesses (khecarīs) draw [the vital energy] upward; of this there is no doubt. They are called the "Directions" (digākhyā).
The Yoginīs, born from the body of Vāmeśvarī and arrogant with their power, attract her who resides there, honor her, and carry her away.
O Maheśvarī, praised by heroes, when enraged, they slay [the enemy] in an instant;
thus has the fivefold movement been described to you.
Pervading the entire body composed of the five elements,
they move through all the apertures by means of the channels, O fair-faced one.
O beautiful one, regarding their entry through all the apertures such as the aperture of space (vyomakūpa) and so forth,
I shall briefly describe those who are the retinues of their respective cakras.
The fierce Ḍāvyāḍāmarikās have resorted to the earthly element (pārthiva-tattva);
by them he is drawn forth—this very sign of the hundred-fold, I shall now declare.
In such a person, there arise pain in the bladder, obstruction of the rectum, fistula-in-ano,
hemorrhoids, and dysentery.
Having understood this, the lord of yogins should perform the remedial rite therein;
for there are the Vyañjinī, the Śākinī, and the Gocarī who have resorted to the Gaṇas.
By means of those [mantras], you shall attract that very person; O fair-faced one, his body will manifest symptoms such as colic, cough, dizziness, and asthma.
Then, one should perform the rite of praise there with the signs of such realization: the whirlwind of wind, the upward flow, and likewise the great milking.
O fortunate lady, facial pain, as well as inflammation of the eyes and ears,
and suffering occurring in the teeth and ears, arises in all the bodily apertures.
The touch of a minor Śākinī lasts for a number of days equal to the month [of her influence];
these are the characteristics of one who has been drawn in by them.
O Goddess of the gods, one should thus perform the counter-measure for that consciousness;
indeed, the host of mice and other creatures is presided over by the assembly of Khecarīs.
This is the characteristic of one who has been drawn by the navel:
he shall suffer from headaches and be afflicted by the *kamalālūta* disease.
By these names they are to be known; among them, the remedy for the fourth [state] is as follows:
the supreme divine host is red and delights in attracting her.
Having encountered various [beings], they know them and destroy them out of malice;
thus has the characteristic of the fivefold [category] been described to you.
Listen now to the sequence by which they take that life-force:
having caused affliction to the self-abiding [prāṇa], they draw out the host of deities residing in the exterior.
Residing within the body in the five cakras, they seize the life-force and abandon it; "one may live even by piercing the navel," such is the supreme command of the Lord.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, you have described that which is great and terrifying,
the multitude of deities residing within the body, in which the individual soul (jīva) is established.
O Destroyer of Kama, tell me how protection is established,
so that when a yogi is well-guarded, he is not overcome on the surface of the earth.
The illustrious Bhairava said:

Listen, O Goddess, as I tell you everything concerning those whose souls are devoted to the practice of yoga, beginning with their teachers, deities, and the sacred fire, and ending with their devotion.
49a) They protect those established in the conduct and observances of the samaya under the Lord of the Gods;
they likewise protect one who practices truth and purity, and who is free from greed and other such vices.
They protect that non-conceptual hero like their own son—
he who is free from violence and slander, and always devoid of idle talk.
O beautiful one, they protect those endowed with compassion for all beings,
but they do not protect those who have fallen from family conduct and are possessed by deceit.
There will be malicious beings who revile [the teachings], yet they will observe the conduct of the samaya;
there will be inferior beings who know solitude, but are awakened by wrong understanding.
O fair-browed one, the rays of Śiva’s command utterly consume those who are arrogant, deficient in devotion, and the lowest of men due to their greed and laziness.
O Goddess praised by heroes, there is no doubt that they kill [the enemies] by means of the terrible command;
yet one who is protected by the weapon-mantra through the ritual procedure of Mṛtyuñjaya remains safe.
One does not encounter the fear of death; hear now the remedy for that as well:
loss, grief, negligence, agitation, and even downfall.
O lady of beautiful hips, these arise for him; there is no protection for him.

That great power of action which was previously described by me— The resulting state is as follows: tasya jāyanti suśroṇi nāstyasya parirakṣaṇam | yā sā pūrvaṃ mayā khyātā kriyāśaktirmahābalā || O lady of beautiful hips, these [obstacles] arise for him; there is no protection for him. That great power of action which was previously described by me—[is now overcome].
The form, possessing five hundred colors, resides in the vehicle of Sadāśiva;
its sound extends from the soles of the feet to the top of the head, resembling blazing flames.
Having meditated upon her head once more, O Bhadrā, she, possessing a radiance like a mass of snow,
fills her own station, performing a great act of expansion.
This protection has been taught by me through the yoga of meditation at the three junctions of the day;
even one who is constantly engaged in such meditation shall attain immortality.
The Night-Teacher is the Great Vidyā, the leader of all vidyās;
O Great Goddess, she who devours the ten is made tenfold for a single purpose.
But when obstructed by the earthly element (pārthiva), it is protected fivefold within the sacrificial fire;
by mere utterance alone, it goes to its own place, free from dissolution.
O King, these five, having reached the state of gases, are successively obstructed within the spheres of earth,
water, fire, and space, O lady of beautiful hips.
Richly endowed with the splendor of a blazing fire, she stood there, radiating light in all directions;
her supreme luster filled the vast expanse of the stainless sky, and from that, it further filled those [beings] upon the earth.

O fair-limbed one, having first performed the worship of the feet [of the Lord], she spent half a year entirely emaciating her body with a flood of tears; then, with a single-pointed mind, she abandoned all supports for the notion of being a mere animal.
Through his grace, she became a knower of reality, free from fear and sorrow.

O Gaurī, having conquered death, he enters the pure path by means of the sequence of the way; having understood the path of the stages, he then enters the central lamp situated within the great abode of existence, or else immediately thereafter.
Free from all disparagement, he has transcended the path of meditative absorption;
that he attains accomplishment by the complete fulfillment of his own stage is nothing surprising here.
Protecting his own body, the best of practitioners attains success;
such is the incomparable majesty of this Vidyā, O Supreme Goddess.
50b) It must be painted and kept strictly secret if one desires long life;
she who transcends all states of reality and is the supreme leader of all those worthy of praise.
Excluding the lamps of light, she resides upon the seat of Kulakaula;
in the form of both the supreme and the non-supreme, she has attained dissolution into the supreme reality.
O Goddess, you bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and you are the releaser from all bonds;
[you are] equal to thousands of horse-sacrifices and likewise to the destruction of [the cycle of] Brahma.
Practiced once, this [mantra], playful upon the tip of the tongue, bestows liberation and shall destroy [all obstacles].
Now, O Mahātapa, listen to the method for protection according to this procedure.
For those who have conquered the steed and abide at the end of the Kula and in the midst of the Kaula,
neither the host of deities nor death shall prevail.
But for those who have attained full cultivation, no manifestation [of faults] is ever perceived;
therefore, there is no obstacle for them as they abide in eternal bliss.
O Bhairavī, having filled the essences of the rays of light with the fire,
and having contemplated them through the vision of the supreme face, one should [perceive] that very essence which is free from affliction.
O beautiful lady, by this procedure one undoubtedly attains a state of well-being.
Now, O beloved, I shall explain another supreme mystery.
O fair-eyed one, out of affection for you, I shall fully explain that which, by the mere knowledge of it, the lord of yogis is not overcome.
O Maheśvarī, beginning from the power of movement (cara-śakti) up to the Vajra-holder (vajrādhāra),
having caused a mass of flames to arise, make that reality a casket (saṃpuṭa).
When one’s upward-pointing crest-lock (*śikhā*) is afflicted by some calamity due to its differentiation,
that external affliction should be dispelled by means of mantra, joined with the meditation on the vajra.
By means of the first [mantra], all that is performed becomes composed of vajra;
situated within the maṇḍala of one's own meditation, it becomes identical with that, like a vajra.
Having meditated on the fifth [syllable] everywhere, one should bring about mastery;
and having first performed the arrangement of the seat, the yogi should apply himself [to the practice].
Listen now to the true nature of the seat consisting of the arrangement of the five mandalas:
it is as white as a lotus tossing amidst the waves in the center of the Ocean of Milk.

51b) One should contemplate [the mandala] as being endowed with the moon and the pericarp, beginning with *nabha* and beginning with *vibha*. Indeed, the fourfold expansion is joined with the elephants ending in *jāḍya*.
The supreme waters extend as far as the fourfold established lotus;
seated there, the great yogi should seek this most excellent sacrifice.
O auspicious lady, one should worship daily; before long, the vajra will arise.
O goddess, he shall be invincible even to the thirty gods, free from old age, disease, and fear.
O Great Goddess, possessing the power of death at will and accompanied by all the yoginīs, he dissolves into the supreme state, which is like food.
This supreme secret has been revealed out of affection for you;
through a year's practice, the hero [attains] the fivefold host of deities.
Established in the division of the five forms and colored by the function of their own parts, they attain perfection through that very state of being composed of them; of this there is no doubt.
O highly fortunate one, they bestow vast enjoyments, their own supernatural powers, and their cities,
delighting the lord of heroes with the splendor of their own palaces.
52a) These very [energies] of Bhairava worship him constantly;
therefore, one whose soul is detached from worldly enjoyment should show them respect.
O Maheśānī, after twelve years he shall depart taking the *piṇḍa* with him;
and it becomes subtle, O highly fortunate one—there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Endowed with the powers beginning with *aṇimā* and honored by the scriptures of Śiva,
the great yogi remains established in the state of peace, joined with that which was previously described.
O Goddess, having attained the body through the complete accomplishment of yoga, this very Śiva himself shall move about at his pleasure and partake in liberation.
O Bhairavī, by this method, one gradually attains subtlety,
even after many hundreds of millions of kalpas spent endowed with various enjoyments.
O Goddess praised by heroes, [the practitioner] dissolves into the supreme reality by his own will.
Thus, this supreme protection has been declared to you here out of devotion.
If it was previously propitiated by you, it has been hidden by that very [deity];
therefore, for the sake of protection, I shall tell you another [method] in brief.
Listen, O portion of the supreme Vidyā: for a yogi who is devoid of recitation (jāpa), whether for himself or for another, that which is merely written [is effective].
Seated upon the Āsana beginning with Nabhā, one should first [place] the Earth element beginning with Sādi and Īśādi.
Complete, accompanied by the neck, situated in the middle of the year and the elements,
enclosed by the king of eyes, and encircled by the half-moon.
O fortunate one, it is unmanifested as eight [syllables], protected by the king of mantras (netrarāja),
endowed with sixteen digits, and encircled by the enclosure of the moon.
O Dear One, one should place that [mandala] endowed with sixteen petals on its exterior.
At the edge of the petal, within the pericarp, the two eyes are formed into a royal fold;
one should gradually pronounce the Bindu and Nāda, and sequentially apply the phonemes according to the threefold thread, wrapping them and fixing them in place.
I have taught the protection of the jar, which is the supreme protector of all;
by what metal or by what mineral [should it be made], O fair-faced one?
One should always wear this amulet; it constantly protects, O beautiful one.
This protection is a great protection that destroys all calamities.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Kulesāra.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, previously you spoke of the supreme bath that conquers death;
O Bhairava, O God, I have now beheld that protection by means of the weapons."
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim a most wonderful secret,
by the mere knowledge of which one is liberated from all defects.
O Goddess, this supreme consecration of heroes is the ultimate conqueror of death;
it subdues poverty and destroys even great diseases.
