With teeth resembling the moonlight and nails like mirrors,
they were adorned with all ornaments and endowed with divine garlands and garments.
Their betel-leaves were exquisite, their speech was charming and full of grace,
and their words flowed like nectar, bringing delight to all.
O Goddess, for those whose minds have reached destruction like the color of a frog,
cause them to rise again by means of a torrent of clouds during the rainy season.
Through charming conversation and conciliation, they entice the practitioner;
yet they do not manifest any physical transformations or provocative gestures that would arouse passion.
Those who display and speak of the state brought about by the flower-bow [of desire] toward you are false;
therefore, for them there is an eternal destination in hell.
Having struck you, who were absorbed in meditation, with a heartless blow, he has been consumed by you;
yet the practitioner of this rite shall attain success through various enjoyments and flavors.
In the presence of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, and Asuras,
as well as Vidyādharas, this great garden is free from the uselessness of birth and suffering.
And due to the non-avoidance of killing women, one is cooked in the hells;
moreover, they sing and dance before the practitioner.
When the hero does not waver even when others display many such transformations intended to remove his pride, then, at the arrival of the auspicious moment, he attains perfection.
Then, by means of heroes, lords of heroes, and yoginīs established in yoga,
she who is firm in her vow attains perfection without effort within three years.
Thus, this ritual procedure for the Goddess, which bestows accomplishment when performed in brief,
brings her to a state of worship within one month once she has taken refuge in her own abode.
For two months, the king is under control; for three months, the common people and the priest likewise; and for that duration, the country itself remains naturally subject to him.
Within six months, the earth girt by the oceans shall be accomplished for him;
therefore, the high-souled lord of heroes should perform this with reverence.
For the desire to attain mastery of the sky and for the accomplishment of the *piṇḍa*,
one should indeed accomplish the *piṇḍa*, which is the unsurpassed mantra of the Goddess.
O Goddess, this supreme secret, which was exceedingly hidden, has now been revealed.
Now follows another [aspect] of the King of Mantras belonging to the Goddess Adharā.
Having adopted silence, the wise one should practice meditation fixed on the state [of the Self];
with his mind focused solely on the vital breath, he attains success within six months.
Likewise, [the yogi] creates a living body and a physical form, the supreme extraction of the essence of mercury,
entry into another's body, and the transformation of one's own form and so forth.
One should accomplish whatever other rites there may be, such as those beginning with *kṛta*;
by performing them at the time of the *visṛjya-nāda-saṃdhyā*, there is nothing that one cannot accomplish.
Having removed the letter *repha* (the *r*) from that,
O beautiful one, one should strike the interior of the secret cave with the arrow-weapon ending in the syllable *phaṭ*, thereby bursting open the knot.
Having thoroughly churned the life-subduing food by means of the supreme *ṛ* syllable,
one should attract much blood with the extremely subtle *sūṃ* syllable.
If one practices that which resides in the *taśkarā*, then, O Goddess, having attained its true nature through the sequence,
the practitioner who accomplishes the *vimarda* [stage] shall cut and bind it.
The two channels are the root of the *vajra*, circular below the *lolā*;
these five are situated within the five knots in successive order.
Having seized those to be divided and having well-informed himself, he should bring them under his control;
thus, O Goddess, he brings even gods, asuras, and humans under his own power.
Having aimed at the supreme target, which consists of the knots to be pierced in due order,
one likewise enters the city of another through those and other applications.
O fair-browed one, O beautiful lady, I have briefly stated the procedure that follows the established tradition; abandon further prolixity.
68b) Now, O beloved, I shall proclaim another supreme secret:
O Goddess, the practitioner of the vow should have a tube made of copper during the Puṣya asterism.
Having taken human testicles and the eyes of a cat,
combined with *srotāñjana* and *sauvīraka*, [one should apply it].
Having filled that tube with flowers on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
he placed it upon the heart of the corpse, which remained smeared with the residue of the poison.
Having applied collyrium to his eyes, the supreme practitioner beholds this entire wheel of living beings— wherever it is worshipped and wherever it is experienced.
Fire is equal to you; so too are heat, the crow, the owl, the jackal, the dog, the cat, the Rākṣasa, the swan, and many others of various kinds.
Whatever edible food fit for humans is found there bestows success;
likewise, its excrement, flesh, fat, skin, and all else grant success.
The rest, O Goddess, are useless; what purpose is served by drawing [them]?
Taking a reed-stalk by its name alone, one should offer water with a flower.
Having filled his penis with that [substance], one should deposit it into the womb of a woman;
then, having burnt it together with two types of collyrium, one should again reduce it to its remaining residue.
O Maheśvarī, having taken [the substance] and consecrated it with the goddess-mantra one hundred thousand times, there is no doubt that one shall behold treasures situated within the earth.
And by taking various and manifold juices, O beloved, one attains success.
Thus has the ultimate truth been shown to you; therein, this incomparable state of mine is like the leaves of the *nāga* tree.
With the nature of worldly existence departed, the path of enjoyment stands before me, free from darkness; it is inconceivable, and one should meditate upon that state through contemplation.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the Kulasāra.
The Goddess said:
O Supreme Lord, that which you have spoken is free from worldly activity, censured by all living beings, and produces delusion when contemplated.
The collection of substances and so forth, as well as those substances which are loathsome—
know these to be the causes of bondage for the mind.
O Hara, the mind that is free from impurity rises above all taints, and through the purification of the mind, that fruit is attained; however,
those with crooked minds fall into hell due to the division of their fundamental nature.
How is it accomplished here by those who, knowing yoga, have entered the family?
O God, explain this to me so that my lack of understanding may be removed.
The illustrious Bhairava said:

The non-dual [reality] has been taught for the followers of the Vedas, the Siddhānta scriptures, the Buddhists, and the proponents of the Ārhata doctrine; yet, being deluded, they do not understand it.
The drinking of *surā* is prescribed in the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice, and the killing of a Brāhmaṇa in the *Puruṣamedha*;
however, that same rule is recorded as being for a Kṣatriya in the *Rājasūya* and in marriage.
In the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), one indeed slaughters the horse; such is the slaughter of animals.
For the sake of a woman's negligence, he who has produced his own offspring casts them away.
That which is extracted is purifying, while that which is not extracted is impure; that which is churned from difficulty is inferior, and that which arises from a single source is devoid of essence.
That which is devoid of supreme bliss is not considered the highest purity;
even after offering oblations to the gods and giving gifts to the ancestors and friends.
O twice-born one, the best of the twice-born eat the remains of the oblation among the gods;
their ascent to heaven occurs like that of lowing cows, O twice-born one.
Each individual difficult deed is great and hair-raising;
every supreme evil is established within the ritual procedure of the void.
Having consumed what is unfit for consumption, one may become intoxicated and even arrogant; likewise, one may engage in forbidden sexual intercourse and pursue every object of desire.
The Vedic dharma, consisting of sacrifices and other rites, established for the twice-born,
is declared to be the root of dharma and the supreme staircase to heaven.
Having attained heaven with great effort out of a desire for enjoyments and the like,
one who destroys the singular Brahman causes oneself to fall down with great force.
Thus, O Goddess, non-duality has been declared in all the Vedas and in the Buddhist scriptures as well; it is the supreme means for purifying the mind.

Those deluded souls, devoid of the descent of power (śaktipāta), do not know the purification of reality (tattva-śuddhi) and their own purification; having known those two as supreme and non-dual, they [attain liberation].
O Goddess, those who know the non-dual state— the reality of the non-dual moment— and who are devoted to the non-duality of action, fall into the Vedic deities.
O Lord of the Gods, those ministers who, out of greed, perform the non-duality of ritual action without having experienced it through direct perception,
certainly go to hell.
Like aged wild elephants sinking in a terrible mire of birth,
those who do not know the supreme reality perish as they sink away.
Regarding one's own suffering and happiness, life and death, the pleasant and the unpleasant, gold and a clod of earth, the pure and the impure, a son and an enemy; [one should remain equanimous].
He whose intellect is constantly such that he maintains an equal disposition toward his wife, his mother, a cow, and even toward those who wish him ill, both while awake and in dream.
For whom the axe and sandalwood are conceived as equal,
and for whom the false notions of "I" and "mine" have forever ceased— [him I call a sage].
For him, there is no object of attainment among attainable things; neither impurity nor merit, nor sin;
neither edible nor inedible, nor that which is prescribed by rule.
If this essence of the meaning of my merits being recounted here is heard, he shall be liberated from all bonds, both those pertaining to daily rites and those pertaining to occasional rites.
Having thus relied upon this state of being, that which pertains to one joined with reality is explained.
Listen, O Goddess, to how non-duality is non-dual from the perspective of the ultimate truth.
For thus has that state been proclaimed—the Nirvāṇa born of the Sole Hero;
it is to be known as solely beneficial, and for that reason it is called non-dual.
In that regard, having always established existence, there is no second [entity] whatsoever; because one who has abandoned the second is non-dual, it is therefore called "non-duality" (advaita).
For one who abides in supreme non-duality and delights in the non-duality of existence,
the state of non-duality regarding action is indeed called the purification of the self.
O Supreme Goddess, dharma and adharma, as well as day and night,
never attain union with the Self.
O Supreme Goddess, having understood and reflected upon persistence, origination, and dissolution,
as well as the state of being devoid of impurity and the course of that which is diminished, O Sinless One.
In that regard, O large-eyed one, hear now the classification of the substances belonging to Śiva, who is perfect, supreme, and of immeasurable splendor.
His power, known as Icchā (Will), is endowed with those attributes and qualities;
there, having arisen through the great mantras, she [assumed] the body of Sadāśiva.
O Dear One, depending upon the five elements, this entire world, produced from a single seed, remains established in its fivefold causes.
Therefore, this investigation into birth was undertaken based on delusion;
it is like seeking the preservation of a seed from a well-differentiated, pure space that lacks any defining characteristics.
When the One is known, duality is not found; the purpose of the other is the all-pervasive equality.
O Goddess of Gods, that which is seedless is that by which this differentiation has been created.
The latent impression of being an elephant arises from the accumulation of experiences;
for one born from a single seed, how could a second [seed] be obtained?
O illustrious one, you should avoid duality; through equanimity, you should contemplate the world.
O Goddess, the earth is the abode of all things; O sinless one, establish yourself in truth.
Brahmā is the presiding lord here and there, and the dense substance there is composed of that;
for all beings, O Bhairavī, consist of that very essence within both what is edible and what is inedible.
72a) Everything here is purified by the thunderbolt, and duality is not found therein;
that which is called "the state of non-falling" is traditionally held to have Viṣṇu as its presiding lord.
And here, regarding the quality of liquid substances, why is there this duality of what is drinkable and what is not?
The form of the world’s manifoldness is that very brilliance born of the terrible [fire].
Rudra does not act within that which is subject to transformation, nor through conceptualization. Men are said to be Vāyu; they are dependent upon the touch of Vāyu.
Presided over by Īśvara, that indeed is touch; O Goddess, having filled all the apertures, it abides as a pair of touches within the ether.
Īśāna is the supreme Brahman, and he abides as Śiva;
they possess brotherhood in every respect, being neither impure nor dualistic.
From the union [of castes], the formation of a social group occurs among the Brahmin and Kṣatriya lineages;
through the eating of food from one's own cook, there arises a unity consisting of the assembly of the five elements.
He perceived the detachment of beings from their various classes;
therefore, having taken that very [detachment] as his object, he was one whose mind was wondrous.
Having attained the supreme state with a non-conceptual mind,
O beautiful one, by abandoning both duality and non-duality through a state of oneness.
A hero should indeed conduct himself [with vigor] and avoid equanimity;
since equanimity is the root of ignorance, he should therefore avoid it.
O Goddess praised by heroes, all human beings arise from a single womb;
the perception of diversity here is merely a conceptual construction for the sake of worldly existence.
How could Śambhu, who is joined with Yośit (the consort), be the cause of union?
Viṣṇu is in the liṅga, Brahmā is in the bhaga, and Maheśvara is in the sprout.
The infinite deities reside within the pores for the sake of the substance;
the seed is Śakti, the supreme and subtle, while in bliss is Paramaśiva.
O Goddess of the Gods, by that very action beings are certainly liberated;
yet, when conceptual construction arises therein, they do not know the ultimate reality.
O Goddess, the nectar arising from that is pure, purifying, auspicious, cleansing, and bestows liberation; it is perfect knowledge born of discernment.
O Supreme Goddess, sound, touch, taste, form, and smell— indeed,
he who enjoys these objects of the senses is a man who attains success.
At this time, through the process of casting off, these five will indeed perish;
due to their absence, there arises the primordial bliss that is devoid of mental fluctuations.
O Goddess, upon the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, the supreme state arises;
having attained oneness of being, they reach the Self, the Power, and the Supreme Reality.
O Goddess of the gods, at that time one becomes possessed of the body of liberation;
yet, O Gaurī, the lowest of men perceive bondage even within liberation.
Having grown [in this state], enveloped by the darkness of ignorance, they have no doubt that they do not recognize the single reality called the Seed, which bestows auspiciousness.
Though one, he has become manifold for the sake of creation, and not otherwise;
when the purification of reality has occurred, then indeed he is stainless.
The stainless [state] is to be made stainless by the latent impression (vāsanā) which has the form of liberation;
through that stainless impression, the realization of reality arises from the soundless state.
O Goddess of the Gods, for one whose mind is pure, there shall never be bondage;
for one who remains in any state whatsoever, there is liberation alone— of this there is no doubt.
For the embodied soul who has awakened through pure intellect and known reality,
there is no practice of purity other than the contemplation of that reality.
The physical body (piṇḍa) arises from blood and semen, combined with feces, urine, and phlegm.
O sinless one, how can vomiting— which is accompanied by blood, bile, and other humors—
be purified simply by constant washing?
Just as when a stone is being ground it appears to become dust,
yet it undergoes neither destruction nor transformation, so it is with the embodied soul.
Just as charcoal being rubbed or washed with water does not abandon its own nature, so it is with everything belonging to embodied beings.
Externally appearing as ashes by nature, like a firebrand held in the hand,
Kālikā does not leave [the body] even when washed with ash-water.
74a) It is not attained in this world by one who practices purity through the sixth meal-time, nor by the three-night fast, nor by pure recitations or vows.

He who has not entered the ocean of meditation does not attain it in this world through sacrifices, gifts, fierce austerities, recitations, vows, or ascetic practices— even by means of the most excellent purity, O one of excellent purity.
For he has not entered that which is to be meditated upon through meditation.
O highly fortunate one, this is the essence of all reality, like the supreme fist of knowledge;
I shall speak of it, so listen to this in brief.
Regarding purity and conduct, as well as non-duality—especially regarding non-duality—one must not harbor attachment; rather, one should follow the liberated ones, who are imperishable.
O Goddess of the Gods, duality arises from non-grasping even within non-duality;
the world perceives that which is ungraspable, therefore one should avoid it.
O Goddess, when the root of latent impressions (vāsanā) is indestructible, it causes delusion through impurity;
due to this delusion, one falls and revolves in saṃsāra.
Just as the wind follows along without conceptualizing, so does the knower of yoga;
both conceptualization and non-conceptualization belong to the realms of Brahma and liberation respectively.
But two remain as the foremost in great austerity: duality and non-duality.
Duality is fraught with fear for those who are joined to it; therefore, one should completely avoid it.
Having resorted to the state of non-duality, one should maintain the highest steadfastness in non-duality;
for the knower of Yoga, there is no need for the contemplation of Kula and Kaula.
Then, O beloved, he for whom the state of meditative cultivation has dissolved into absorption should be known as one who abides in supreme non-duality within non-duality.
Thus liberated, that yogi who has reached the further shore of yoga liberates others;
for him, duality and non-duality are equal, as he has realized the continuity of reality.
Equal everywhere, pervading all that is real, equal and spontaneously omnipresent;
abiding in equality through equanimity, one enters into the equality of one's own body.
Just as one cannot distinguish another drop of milk within that milk, so too, for him,
there is no distinction between reality and the means of attainment even in hundreds of millions of eons.
75a) When the body has become established through equanimity and has reached a state of partlessness,
he by whom non-duality is cultivated has made the movement firm.
For him, old age and birth exist only as a distant possibility for a limited time;
there is no further return once the seed has reached a state of seedlessness.
There is no yoga higher than *nirbīja*, nor is there any other supreme non-duality (*advaita*),
by which one is permeated with the state of non-duality through the system of *Kula* and *Kaula*.
Just as the supreme, all-pervading nature abides in its own essential form, so too,
through reasoning and the discernment of reasoning, he himself is directly Bhairava.
O lady of excellent hips, such a one is liberated while living and is esteemed by all yoginīs;
this essence of non-duality has been told to you by me, and not otherwise.
Neither non-duality nor duality exists apart from the realization of reality;
having cultivated the essence of supreme non-duality through firm conviction.
For him who possesses purity of being, there is non-duality in ritual actions according to the scriptures, and he is free from hesitation regarding his conduct.
75b) His success shall be without obstacle and liberation itself is certain;
now, moreover, I shall speak again by means of another procedure.

Those who harbor suspicion regarding the mantra, suspicion regarding themselves, and likewise suspicion regarding the ritual substances, are not practitioners; they are merely like those who have reached the age of forty.
As long as they do not find reality;
but once the supreme reality is known, all castes are of the nature of Śiva.
Having realized that Śiva is omnipresent, one is established in the state beyond both caste and non-caste.
The form of bliss resides as Śiva within all castes;
it abides in this world in everything from Śiva down to a gnat.
Bliss through power, bliss through Śiva, and the bliss of pervasiveness are devoid of [duality];
everything is presided over by consciousness and is completely colored by the [supreme] aspect.
But how could there be even a trace of any substance beyond the totality?
For the body consists of the five elements, as do all the substances that reside within it.
He said to them: "What is the nature of those things? Whence comes their purity or impurity?
O Goddess, that which resides within the body of the embodied being remains [there]."
But how, O dear one, can these be reconciled in the interim?
For they emerge from impurity and yet proceed toward me, the immortal.
Arising from one source, they have reached a state of affection for one another;
they have become of one flavor and are augmented by that single essence.
Since it is pervaded by a single reality, how could there be impurity therein?
O Goddess, abandon this mental construction of "mind-only" like chaff.
O Bhairava, abandon the impurity of mind-only and become stainless;
since the mind is the supreme root of both bondage and liberation, purify it with diligent effort.
One whose mind is pure and free from doubt— by being devoid of suspicion,
there shall be no bondage for him, nor any fear in this world or in the next.
For one who contemplates his own body as being struck down, there arises a state of pure awakening through such contemplation.

Having washed the mind— which is free from the stain of doubt, established in the reality of both the real and the unreal, and which follows after all those [objects]— in the stream of the radiance of the sun that is the state of Śiva,
one becomes a vessel for liberation through such practice.
The Goddess Śrī said:
I have heard the entire teaching from the Lord as non-dual in the ultimate sense;
through the continuous flow of hearing, my own mind has been purified.
I bow to that which has washed away the darkness of ignorance, whose sphere transcends conceptual construction,
which has attained equanimity through its very equality, and which, by being thus equanimous, has abandoned all states of being.
Free from delusion and envy, devoid of multiplicity,
lacking both existence and non-existence as well as unity, it is firmly established in true being.
"O best of gods, by your grace my mind has attained immovability;
O Bhairava, I thus perceive even the One as many through its various distinctions."

However, O Supreme Lord, I ask about mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). You have stated that duality exists between the grasper and the grasped; yet you have declared that worship should not be performed without wine and meat.
If one were to entertain even a slight misconception regarding this, it would give rise to delusion.
By your grace, tell me this so that I may understand it without doubt:
what is meant by the designation "kōmada," and what indeed is this called "māṃsa"? Tell me.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! You have asked a supreme question.
O beloved, I shall tell you in brief that which is most secret.
I shall speak very concisely and according to the truth, and not otherwise, regarding the primary substances from which intoxicants and meat arise.
The supreme seed-syllable is indeed "Nāma," which arises from the highest bliss; through its union with the external state of being, it has reached the state of non-attachment.
That very thing, O Goddess, which has been shown, is designated as "flesh";
this substance is declared to be supreme, purifying, and bestowing accomplishment.
O Goddess, one should perform the oblation, partake of it, and satisfy the ancestors and the gods;
the great hero should always offer this in the worship of the mantra.
Whatever collection of substances exists upon the surface of the earth,
all that is offered by him through the offering of meat.
The deities attain satisfaction and the mantra becomes fruitful;
O beautiful one, by that, the sacrifice to Śiva has then been performed by him.
It is said that the Śiva-sacrifice surpasses all other sacrifices;
for it is worshipped, O Bhairavī, by means of the supreme manifestation of the knowledge of mantras.
O Goddess of gods, by that sacrifice one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence;
O Beloved, everything known through that [knowledge] becomes fully accomplished.
O illustrious one, that seventeenth digit which was previously described by me as bestowing supreme immortality is merged within that supreme state.
Inconceivable and beyond description, she bestows supreme immortality;
for the sake of nourishing the world, she remains present within the mandala.
O beautiful one, it was placed in the water of the moon’s radiance for the purpose of nourishing the ancestors, the assembly of gods, and the cycle of living beings through speech.
Abiding as the cause for nourishment, she is established within liquid substances;
through the churning of the midst of the ocean of milk, she has attained manifest individuality.

The state of Vāruṇī should be known; those by whom the asuras have been drunk are remembered as *asurāḥ*. Arising from the primordial principle (*āditattva*), the intoxicants are auspicious in the midst of the drinkable.
Madirā is to be known as that which intoxicates; these [powers] are established in the Śakti and reside in the Ādhāra.
She who bestows the nectar of the left is called the Nectar of the Left;
she is the primordial power Manonmanī, abiding in the form of both the transcendent and the immanent.
She is the producer of bliss, meritorious, and the cause of the state beyond mind (unmanā);
abiding in the moon, she is the drinker of the nectar of the moon and the destroyer of all sins.
O Goddess, the fruit of all sacrifices and the bathing at all sacred fords do not equal even a sixteenth part of that nectar which comes from the mere touch of the Goddess.
From seeing it, obstacles are destroyed; from touching it, there is an accumulation of merit.
Through the offering of food, mantras, and ritual actions, as well as the propitiation of the Guru, the Devas, and the Fire;
Having understood the state of non-sound, O fair-faced one,
and having recognized that supreme source where [the sound] has arisen, one should apply the refined [mantra].
The assembly of deities is her presence, and the mantras abide as her very mouth;
she is the supreme one who bestows eternal bliss and liberates even those bound by wealth.
There is eternal bliss and play, with constant practice at every moment;
established therein is he whose merit and vows consist of the joy of those qualities.
O fair-faced Gaurī, he who is constantly united with that non-conceptual state and perceives it as the substance shall partake in the fruit of accomplishment.
Otherwise, O Goddess, if one partakes out of greed after having recognized it as a mere fraction [of the full measure],
his sin from that drinking results in a descent into hell.
She should always be praised in this way and never reviled;
with this mantra, one should mark her and worship that vessel.
Amṛta, Vāri, and Ākāśa, endowed with thirteen kalās—this is the excellent mantra; from among these, the first is the presiding seed-syllable (vīja).
The word *amṛtau* is proclaimed as the first part, followed by *vāme*; then *ame*, and at the end *namaḥ*. This is celebrated as beginning with the *Tārā* (the syllable Om).
Thus, by remembering and meditating upon her as the Immortal (Amṛtā), she then becomes the source of prosperity; even when drunk,
she shall liberate a living being, even one who has performed evil deeds.
She was also drunk by all the deities, the two Ṛṣis, and the Mātṛguhyakas.
These were placed upon the earth by the Lord for the sake of uplifting cyclic existence;
they belong to the lineage of the Siddhas for the sake of the accomplishment of the assembly of heroes, and not to any other lineage.
For the sake of Vedic sacrifices, it is a continuous flight of stairs to heaven;
therefore, these two substances are indeed the most excellent among all substances.
It should be given for the purpose of worship, fire-rituals, and honoring the Guru on festive occasions;
especially so when making offerings to heroes and during the worship of the circle of Yoginīs.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Kulasāra.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme procedure for conduct,
by the mere knowledge of which the practitioner’s doubts are severed.
O Goddess, I wander for the sake of attaining perfection; therefore, listen to that in its true essence:
greed, delusion, anger, and likewise egoism.
One should avoid these first, and only thereafter begin the practice.
I shall explain their distinctions; listen, O large-eyed one!
Tālaka, Cuṃvaka, Cārvāka, and likewise Ūrādhāka;
Śiva is declared to be Bhūtamanaḥ, and the practitioner (sādhaka) is also of five types.
Tālaka is said to be Gūḍha, and likewise Cuṃbaka is Udaka;
Cārvāka is declared to be Daiśika, and Ārādhya is one who has resorted to a sacred seat (pīṭha).
The practitioner (sādhaka), though consisting of five divisions such as Śiva, Udbhava, Jaha, Unmatta, and so forth,
is designated as a "sādhaka" because of his state of being intent upon spiritual practice (sādhana).
One should accomplish the various siddhis established within the path of the Kula;
the practice of the Kula is deliberated upon by those who are well-guarded and deeply devoted.
The observer of the vow should wander through the three types of realms: the village, the country, and likewise the inner self;
as well as at Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, and Oḍḍiyāna—these being the three.
O lady of excellent vows, the yogin [should dwell] briefly in the sacred seats (pīṭhas) within the fields of the deceased;
thus has the collection of fields, sub-fields, and junctions been described to you in brief.
80a) O beautiful one, I shall proclaim the inheritance that brings happiness to practitioners;
the seat (pīṭha), O Saṃdarī, is threefold: to the left, to the right, and in front.
The yogi should wander within that which resides in the body, but should avoid the external;
these three—the knots of passion (rajas), purity (sattva), and darkness (tamas)—are supreme.
For one established by these, the seats (pīṭhas) are accomplished; there is no doubt about this.
For one established upon an eight-petaled lotus, [the seats] are as numerous as the vital breaths (prāṇas).
O Goddess, after twenty [breaths] have passed, the moving twilight (calasaṃdhyā) occurs;
O Dear One, from this movement of the breath, three hundred and sixty [breaths] elapse.
The knower of the vital breath (prāṇa) abides beyond the body, which consists of the sacred seats (pīṭha), secondary seats (upapīṭha), and junctions (saṃdoha);
the reciter of the Haṃsa mantra attains perfection, for there is no room for doubt in this matter.
O Goddess, O Beloved, the movement among them occurs on a path that exists in two states:
one consisting of the tranquil sound (nāda), and the other situated in the Śeṣa and Ajeśvara [realms].
All accomplishments are perfected when one has attained identity with those five;
likewise, the sacred fields, seats, and paths, as well as the moving and stationary beings, are attained by taking the final [element].
O Goddess, O Leader of Heroes, I have thus briefly explained that which bestows all accomplishments; now I shall fully describe the wandering in hell.
Success is achieved by wandering where the goddesses reside,
as well as at the gate of a king, and likewise in places of impurity or strife.
O Goddess of gods, O beautiful one, for one whose body has been purified by knowledge and who has abandoned all longing, the host of deities resides within the reservoirs of water.
Displaying their own bodies as the singular state of the supreme reality,
they go to the secret meeting (melāpa) and bestow the boon upon the practitioner at the appointed signal.
O Goddess of the gods, he becomes auspicious; hear now the procedure according to the truth.
For Unmattalīlāpāda, the fifth is the vow of the moon.
Free from all modes of conduct and established in every form, it is not perceived by the world; O Beloved, such is the state established therein.
This must be practiced by the knower of yoga alone, whether walking or standing;
having abandoned all other states of being, one should remain established in these eight.
81a) But when they are hostile in the midst of the assembly, having abandoned the Kaulika conduct, they laugh, sing, and even play about while looking on.
Subsisting on alms, free from food, and having conquered the pairs of opposites, he should always remain;
he should not fall under the sway of food, nor should he be agitated, but should restrain all beings.

One should remain free from desire for one's own sake, dwelling with a heart that delights in the welfare of others; one should not fall under the sway of delusion, nor should one take refuge in passion.
When he has become dependent on what he receives and eats everything like a crow,
one should cause him to perform there the *akāmya* sacrifice for the sake of his two sons, provided he possesses the capacity.
One should not disturb the power of hunger; desiring to satisfy hunger, one should eat once.
Hunger is not to be deliberated upon; having honored it with the mind, one should eat.
Therefore, one should not grasp this substance as a real entity;
one should not manifest its intrinsic nature, for in this matter there is no doubt that one would be deceived.
But having worshipped the host of deities, O Goddess, when they are directly perceived in an instant and established in their own forms, they are here considered to be merely the granting of boons.
O Mistress of Heroes, when they speak thus, the practitioner should then rise,
pierce their left limbs, and offer them the arghya water.
Having prostrated like a staff before them, one should offer whatever is desired:
mercury, an elixir, a sword, a pill, or sandals.
O Bhairavī, O Sovereign of Heroes, first stand here— whether it be a Vetāla from an anthill, or yellow pigment, or chalk, or even a sacrificial pap (caru).
Having obtained that, O Goddess, one of great intelligence attains perfection with a perfected body;
indeed, one should dissolve even that subtle body into the supreme state during the process of absorption.
No obstacle hinders that lord of heroes engaged in great austerity;
he is focused on his own mind, as well as on others, and likewise knows the sacred fields and seats.
Whether external in the village or internal within oneself, established upon the path— when the practitioner, O Goddess, knows this thus with his senses restrained, he is a true knower.
His success shall be free from obstacles and accompanied by prosperity at every step;
the deities will be honored by that practitioner, of this there is no doubt.
82a) One might wander about merely for the sake of filling the belly of another;
yet one's own purpose is not accomplished, and one is frustrated at every step.
Thousands of obstacles arise for him, there is no doubt;
yet he is a hero, a brave man, majestic, pure of heart, and stainless.
One who has conquered the senses, mastered meditation, observes the conduct of the observance,
keeps the circle of deities well-guarded, has subdued anger, and is firm in his vows.
Laziness, death, wretchedness, malice, and harsh speech;
thirst, sleep, fear, delusion, passion, and even immortality.
O Goddess, he whose body is embraced by you, who are proclaimed as the transformations (vikāras), attains perfection by adopting this conduct; it cannot be otherwise.
O Goddess of the Suras, I shall also describe another variety of practice:
abandon the ash, the linga, and the matted hair; abandon rituals such as the worship of the linga.
Always remaining concealed by a hidden state of being and established in a secret range,
the self-restrained one [should act] with even more secret states of being toward those others.
O Goddess of the gods, for those who know the path, everything indeed perishes; such being the case, O you who abide in the Kula, the Kula-conduct belongs to one established in the Kula.
One is not fit for this in any other way; rather, one must be of the nature of the lineage of the Siddhas.
Listen to that which I shall speak in brief—the sixfold [mantra] that bestows accomplishment.
Always abandoning initiation, exposition, and likewise the accumulation of material goods,
one should avoid public gossip and social assemblies from afar.
One should hold a single staff made of śiṃśapā, khadira, or sāla wood,
measuring four cubits in length, or even half of that.
The alms-bowl should be made from sacrificial trees, measuring ten joints, eight joints, or fifty finger-breadths in length.
Six finger-breadths in height and eight in width,
it may be circular, square, or lotus-shaped according to one's preference.
O beautiful one, the vessel should be made exactly according to the prescribed measurement,
with equal proportions for its parts, and entirely free from knots and the like.
83a) Its circumference is proclaimed to be half of twelve [in measure].
O lady of excellent complexion, I shall now describe the ritual placement (nyāsa) of that staff.
The cubit (hasta) is proclaimed to be a measurement of twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgula), by which, when maintained, one succeeds free from obstacles.
O Bhāgyasundarī, one should perform the arrangement of the five mandalas in four ways for pride and in five ways for fortune,
using the five mantras.
O Goddess, that which consists of twice eight (sixteen) and is situated above all [the elements],
that portion of space— one should place that as the sixteenth.
O fortunate one, the supreme circle of mantras of all the arts is pervaded and situated in the sky; it is brought under control by the flood of nectar.
While being thus worshipped by Śiva and others within the range of the earth,
one who meditates upon that [reality] through spontaneous play shall become excluded from death.
Freed from all obstacles, one attains accomplishment; there is no doubt in this matter.
The great-souled Kriyāśakti measures fifty finger-breadths.
Each finger should be placed separately, and at its end is the supreme meditation;
O fair-faced one, with the mind absorbed in that meditation, it is just as before.
O Goddess, one should place the eight-limbed, all-pervading goddess upon the eight joints;
O Great Goddess, on the ten joints, she is characterized by the ten syllables.
One should install [the deity] with supreme devotion within the Great Heat (mahātapa), which is absorbed in the Supreme;
or else, through devotion, one may perform the installation of the latent impressions (vāsanā) by means of perfumes, incense, offerings, and so forth.
One should perform worship regularly and on special occasions, and always remain capable of meditation;
having unified them within one's own body, they are made to attain a state of equal flavor through the principles (tattvas).
One should indeed apply the supreme punishment like a staff against those who are not established in the ultimate reality;
however, for one who is fit, the application of yoga bestows yoga and is celebrated as the giver of yoga.
O lady of excellent vows, the remaining [syllables] should be distributed fivefold according to the previous arrangement;
O Goddess of the gods, the method for the sixfold [arrangement] has thus been explained to you.
O Mistress of Heroes, at the time of initiation, his meditation is said to be twofold:
[first], the power of the surging waves of fire; [second], the female serpent [emerging] from the aperture.
Having meditated and worshipped with all ritual offerings through the application of meditative absorption,
he should place that [substance] into the hand of the disciple and cause him— whose senses are overwhelmed— to drink it.
O Great Goddess, the rite of nourishment is prescribed from the preceding meditations;
by means of that, the rite of raising [the deity] should be performed, as well as the rite of immortalization.
Whether one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine [beings] are connected there, for all of them there is initiation; of this there is no doubt.
They fall when there is a transition of the vital breath (*jāna*) and when the fetters are loosened;
therefore, O best of goddesses, the *pradam* must always be maintained by the Kaulika.
Having placed the supreme Kriyā-śakti of great power within the alms-bowl,
O lady of beautiful hips, one should place it eightfold externally in the middle region.
The Goddess who bears the eight forms, when installed, is the destroyer of obstacles;
having again inflamed her with sound through supreme contemplation,
she becomes the supreme Kauḍilini, made immortal by all the waters.
He whose belly is like a sacrificial pit contains this entire world, both moving and unmoving.
Therefore, it is known as Kauṇḍilī; I do not manifest otherwise.
O Bhairavī, those substances which are deposited in that [place] are indeed pure.
By consuming these sacrificial oblations (caru), attainment is surely achieved; of this there is no doubt. One is not overcome by poisons, great diseases, or obstacles.
O Goddess, for one who remains outside of contact with others and stays constantly wandering, even without [the practice], sleep occurs after twelve [muhūrtas].
O Bhairava, by this procedure, the practitioner’s offering of clarified butter, performed with wood free from defects,
is accomplished along with all supernatural powers.
O Goddess, O Gaṇāmbikā, listen now; the arrangement of the locks and so forth has been declared as fivefold—external and internal—by Maṇḍa.
O beloved Mistress of Heroes, perception is said to be fivefold; it is causal for ordinary beings, but that which arises from yoga is described by me to you, O Yoginī.

The striker (tālaka) strikes the hollows, which are the causes of the forms of sense-objects; the mind, however, assumes the reflection [of those objects] within the single path that leads to cessation.
Therefore, the lord of yogis, who is a marvel of yoga, has declared it "Kālakam";
one should impel the path at Cumbaka through the sequence beginning with Udāna and so forth, step by step.
Because it unites the knots of the granthi, it is called the *cuṃvaka*;
the *cārvāka* should chew all the sense organs that follow the mind.
O Queen of the Gods, stability has been proclaimed by the Cārvāka through the breath,
or otherwise through good character, oneness, and so forth.
The seat (*pīṭha*), severed from discursive thought and established as the support of all, is to be known as beginningless; the yogi who follows this path attains the state of liberation.
Arisen from Śiva, become Śiva, and established in the principle of Śiva (śivatattva),
it pervades all paths and is, from the beginning, the support of all as the partless (niṣkala).
Consisting of that mind and absorbed in it, he has reached the cessation of all states of being;
there are no senses, nor indeed vital breath, nor any object of contemplation, nor even the act of contemplation.
To the one arisen from the exhaustion of all phenomena, the well-ascertained absence of a stake;
who is stainless, free from passion, pure, uniquely supreme, and free from affliction.
Having taken recourse to the non-existence of all things, which itself has no support in the non-existence of all things,
one should thus contemplate one's own self as being composed of that within all existing things.
Then, having attained identity with that which is changeless like Śiva,
O beautiful one, he was present in front, behind, on the sides, and indeed below.
When that mind becomes identical with Him through an unchanging state of being, one should be regarded as arisen from Śiva; like Śiva himself, one should wander the earth.
Thus, O Supreme Goddess, by means of this fivefold yoga,

those born of Śiva attain [liberation] through the five elements according to their bodies; O Supreme Sovereign, just as the body of Śiva is born of Śiva, so too are the devotees of Śiva (śaivas) born of Śiva.
O Bhairavī, I shall describe their [varieties] according to the divisions of tālaka and so forth.
Tālaka is Sadyomūrti, while Cuñcuka is Vāc;
Cārvāka is declared to be Ghora, and Puruṣa is remembered as Ārādhya.
Thus, the five divisions beginning with Śivodbhūta and Īśa are proclaimed;
in this manner, the kalās, mantras, objects, and instruments are likewise constituted.
O illustrious lady, the fifth itself becomes the dissolution of the fivefold [categories] through the sharp edge arising from Śiva, which severs all distinctions whatsoever.
He was declared by the Lord of all to be the remainder through his sport;
like Śiva, he is omnipresent, and like Kṛtānta, he is the devourer of all.
Like a mute in the assembly of people seeking his faults,
like a thunderbolt in piercing the truth, he is impenetrable by all beings.
But because of their greed for meat, even the mother held fast to the moon, the skin,
the peacock feather, and likewise the clarified butter according to their own nature.
If one does not contemplate that which has been established, it is like being bound by a sword;
therefore, meditation is conquered [only] when there is transparency like a piece of soft crystal.
Like water placed in the midst of water, he has attained a state of oneness;
like a dog, he indulges in desire and does not discriminate regarding food.
Having become free from passion for desire, one should not mentally dwell upon the objects of desire;
Savīra and Vīranātha are regarded as accomplished masters by the Yoginīs.
He, born of Śiva, is to be saluted and honored by Śiva;
he is liberated while living, always and in every state, in accordance with reality.
Thus, O Goddess of the Gods, I have explained to you all the various modes of conduct pertaining to the lineage of the Siddhas,
O auspicious one, which follows the tradition of the Siddhakaulas.
But he who is concealed within the practice of conduct (caryā), which accomplishes liberation,
acts for the purpose of the task of attaining the *piṇḍa*, being colored by the nature of the Supreme.
O Gaurī, what else shall I say? It bestows absorption in that [Reality] and removes every impurity; tell me, has this not been considered?
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Kulasāra.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, how are the jewels heard of as being born from the lineage-mothers?
How is it known that they are not otherwise, both manifest and unmanifest? Please explain this.
If there is existence, how can there be non-existence? If there is non-existence, practice meditation. In existence, destruction occurs; in non-existence, there is no defining characteristic.
Devoid of characteristics, without support, and established in non-existence—
whether manifest or unmanifest, numbered or even beyond number.
What is their purpose, or by what means do they attain the status of jewels?
O Lord, tell me the value of these jewels so that I may be free from doubt.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Mother of the Universe, O Triyambikā, the sustainer of the world, you who are the agent of cause and effect—why do you weep with your throat constricted? What is this wonder?
That which has not been told to anyone, that which is the supreme secret—
all of that has been told to you, both in brief and in detail.
One's own power and that of another are proclaimed as the third;
that is the essence of the Three Jewels, while the rest is merely its own nature.
From Brahmā down to Śiva, the entire aggregate of principles,
colored by various forms and transformations, follows along.
Through arising, persistence, and destruction, and through the bondage of karma consisting of the qualities (guṇas) and so forth,
there occurs a transformation of the pure [self] by means of its mere appearance as a reflection.

O Beloved, for one who is established in reality, absorbed in it, and identified with it, there is no perception of duality; here, even the pair of "one" and "many" does not exist as something separate from the Self.
For it is precisely this that a person constantly wanders through in saṃsāra;
by the destruction of that [ignorance], his desire ceases, and he no longer wanders while remaining in the world.
It is surrounded by powers such as will, knowledge, and action;
it understands heaven, liberation, hell, and the fall from those states.
O Goddess, O Vīreśī, what has been spoken by me to you is not otherwise;
awakened, O Goddess, one perceives the reality of Śiva on all sides.
O sinless one, everything has been filled by him through his own power and by his own will;
because it bestows the realization of Śiva, it is celebrated as the *Śivatattva*.
O Bhairavī, that jewel which is delightful with all jewels and bestows omniscience—
she should be known as having that as her cause within the principle of Śiva.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, that eye of mine [has been purified] by the jewel-ornament of that which reveals the supreme reality, through subsequent meditative cultivation. 88a)
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Meditation brings about the realization of the absence of both [subject and object];
through non-nourishment, self-cognition proceeds uninterrupted.
When consciousness is free from nourishment and has been thoroughly cultivated as pure awareness (ciciti),
then, upon the cessation of mental cultivation, it perceives the imperishable Śiva along with the jewels.
One who lacks reflection and whose mind is fixed on others cannot extract [the essence],
for without being bound to that state, it cannot be manifested without those [conditions].
O dear one, the union of these two is declared to be for the sake of Dharma;
for one who contemplates the purpose of Dharma, its non-existence would be a disaster for you.
O Goddess, through constant and true contemplation, Śiva is the imperishable jewel of the self;
"ātmaratna" is proclaimed as a second synonym for him.
In the ultimate sense of the Dharma, the true nature of things is the state of pure gnosis alone;
beyond that, all consciousness is by its very nature the essence of the mind.
Having abandoned the state of existence within non-existence by demonstrating the meaning of the syllables,
that [reality] is realized as a state of oneness through the most profound states of being.
Through the attainment of Śiva by means of the jewel of power (śaktiratna), it is proclaimed as a "jewel";
O Goddess, this triad of jewels bestows yoga upon yogins.
O Goddess, what need is there for other causes when this [practice] is established here?
It must be guarded with great effort, just as one would guard wealth from thieves.
The solar [mantra], however, is perceived by others and illuminates all jewels;
O highly fortunate one, the Three Jewels must not be given to one who has not been examined.
It should be given to one who is tranquil, devoted to the supreme devotion to Śiva,
who is well-pleased, a hero, and initiated into the Krama.
Having consecrated him according to the ritual procedure and having caused him to hear the family precepts,
[the initiation is granted] to one who abides by the conduct of the samaya, and not otherwise, O Goddess praised by heroes.
Furthermore, O Goddess of the Gaṇas, I shall again proclaim the instruction on the five jewels;
listen as I explain how the one is divided fivefold.
89a) O fair-faced one, that which was proclaimed first is said to be the Holder of the Staff (Daṇḍadhāra).
Through its attainment, there is extreme subtlety; together with the *piṇḍa*, it is the means for liberation.
The eternal [power], possessing the six kalās, is again fivefold:
[bestowing] longevity, nourishment, actions, stability, and the accomplishment of the physical body (piṇḍa).
O beloved, this is the instruction on the five jewels arising from the single jewel;
O Goddess, its state of infinite reality is perceived everywhere.
By restraining others with effort, one attains stability and all perfections;
this jewel of power undoubtedly illuminates all other jewels.
The state of Svaratneśa consists of stability, while Pratiṣṭhā is the state of being absorbed in that;
having become Śiva, one is perceived as nothing other than the jewel of Śiva, the jewel of consciousness.
Just as all rivers and streams find their cessation in the ocean,
so indeed do all jewels come together in that one supreme place.
The classification of gems for your sake has been explained according to their gross and subtle divisions;
they are further divided into five types, from the grossest of the gross down to the subtlest, in five successive stages.
And in the maṇḍala, O Great Goddess, one should contemplate the five jewels;
this is the most essential, the proven, and the lineage with its many points of conviction.
When [the practice] is perfected, that very means of accomplishment is joined with the food;
having purified it with the wind of the *saṃpuṭa*, one should contemplate the self as the *raṃ*.
The knower of yoga perceives everything through the light of the radiance of the jewel of the Self;
the jewel of the Self is Śiva, and the jewel of Power (Śakti) is likewise Śiva in threefold form.
O Vīranātha, the Jewel is proclaimed first;
O Goddess, the power of the Self is threefold, while the Jewel of Power is fivefold.
O Goddess praised by heroes, these fourteen have been fully described; they should be known, O lady of excellent hips, by those who seek knowledge and by those who desire accomplishment, my dear.
The majesty of one's own body is manifested in many ways through various auspicious states, according to the path of the guru’s instruction.
Since that enclosure was then composed of all kinds of jewels, it must be diligently guarded with food,
edibles, meals, and drinks, as well as weapons, ornaments, and decorations.
90a) One should not cause bodily affliction through practices such as fasting;
for the *pavitra* and the concluding rites (*pāraṇa*) are the highest of all things for the sake of peace.
He by whom one's own *piṇḍa* is known is liberated; he is Śiva, the imperishable.
Therefore, O fair-eyed one, it must be understood with every effort.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Kulasāra.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, O Goddess of the Gods, I shall fully explain the different types of *lakṣas*,
by the mere knowledge of which all this is successfully accomplished.
Whether it be a jewel or even a non-jewel, one who does not apply himself to yoga gains nothing at all;
O fortunate lady, without the *lakṣa*, all this is useless.
I shall explain its divisions as they are established through those divisions:
the internal aim, the external aim, and likewise the aim on both sides.
He is remembered as being external, internal, other, and yet another, beyond all marks;
he who knows these five marks attains the fruit of perfection.
And liberation itself is established as directly perceptible, without a doubt;
therefore, O Supreme Goddess, one should know the knowledge of the defining characteristics (lakṣajñāna), as well as yoga.
Initiation, consecration, transference, and departure [of the soul], as well as entry into another's body, [and so forth]... O Sage!

That [attainment] proceeds through the conquest of all one hundred thousand varieties by means of the *raja-maṇḍala*, sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), and so forth, as well as numerous mudrās, oblations, and recitations.
That which is accomplished through journeys to great cremation grounds and through rites of formidable practice is not achieved by one who remains in hardship or in a state of suffering.
He who knows the *lakṣa* is omniscient; he is a yogi who has reached the further shore of yoga.
[He knows] the ritual procedure for initiation as well as the transference and removal [of karma].
Discerning the target, he effects both restraint and favor in an instant;
the target is his steadiness, as well as the cultivation of being within that state.
O beautiful goddess, for whomsoever this fourfold set— well-concealed discernment, and the self-abiding of one's own nature— is firmly established by itself;
He is a knower of the Kula, a Kula-teacher, and indeed one who knows the Kula-conduct; he is a knower of both Akula and Kula— he alone is worthy to perform initiation.
Having established a steady intellect and having restrained the mind with effort, one should remain composed.
Listen to the essence of the *lakṣa*: that jewel is [made of] Kāśika silk. Its first internal *lakṣa* has four divisions.
But by one who knows the application of ritual action, the firm *sāla* tree is to be treated in four ways.
Indeed, stability arises from a hundred thousand [recitations] without [interruption];
therefore, O auspicious lady, through that, grace is bestowed upon each hundred thousand.

O Gaurī, that which remains in the midst of the *yāvana* [state], even in the hair (*vālaka*), is established; where the beginning of the hair is, make that which moves firm. [This pertains to] the fourfold *lakṣa* of the Conqueror (*Ajita*).
O Goddess, the people are elsewhere; in that very place, stability arises through the two steps.
The End
